chapter_theme: Indra's festival at Puhar: a survey of the city's two quarters and the market between them, the warrior women's possessed blessing and the warriors' head-offerings at the guardian spirit's altar, the halls brought from the north by Thirumavalavan, the five marvellous courts that guard against theft, disease, hidden wrong and a bent sceptre, the bathing of Indra and the rites of all the gods; then Kovalan roaming with Madhavi, the festival's women seen as moon, lotus and Death in disguise, and the omen of Kannaki's and Madhavi's throbbing eyes.

cast.role: the unnamed reigning Chola king of Puhar, for whose victory and welfare the rites are made
the guardian spirit sent by Indra to remove the Chola king's distress, worshipped at its altar in the market
the women of the old warrior houses who dance possessed and bless the king
the fighting men of Maruvur and Pattinappakkam who offer themselves at the altar
a Chola king of the past remembered for his northern campaign to the Himalaya
the king of the Vajra country who gave Valavan a pavilion as tribute
the king of Magadha who, defeated, gave Valavan a hall of debate
the king of Avanti who gave Valavan an arched gateway in friendship
the spirit of the crossroads (பூத சதுக்கம்) that seizes and devours wrongdoers
the five great councils of the king, acting together at the festival
the eight groups of royal attendants, acting together at the festival
son of the merchant Maasaathuvan, Kannaki's husband, now living with Madhavi
the dancer of Puhar with whom Kovalan lives
Kovalan's wife, daughter of the merchant Maanaaygan
Kama, the bodiless god of love, whose army of festival beauty assails the town

silappathikaram:5:1-15.reading: The sun, rising over the mountain and lifting the dark cloak from the earth pictured as a woman with the sea for dress and hills for breasts, lights up Puhar's terraced mansions, its storerooms, the rich men's houses, the quarter by the harbour where Yavanas live, the shore settlements of foreign traders who came with the ships, and the streets where scents, powders, sandal, flowers and incense are hawked.
silappathikaram:5:1-15.nuance: The catalogue of Maruvurppakkam begins with the outsiders: the Yavanas whose quarter dazzles onlookers are called people who do not know how things are used (பயன்அறிவு அறியா), and the foreigners are those who came with the ships' wealth and stay mingled with the town. Puhar is first a port.
silappathikaram:5:1-15.unit_note: Moved the end from line 16 to line 15: line 15 closes the item 'the town streets where they hawk scents' (நகர வீதியும்), while line 16 begins the weavers' item that ends on line 17.

silappathikaram:5:16-39.reading: The catalogue goes on through the weavers of silk, hair and cotton, the broad streets heaped with cloth, coral, sandal, agil, pearls, gems and gold beyond measuring, the grain street, the sellers of cakes, toddy, fish, salt and meat, the brass-smiths, coppersmiths, carpenters, blacksmiths, painters, potters, goldsmiths, jewellers, tailors and leather-workers, the great bards who play the seven notes faultlessly, and the makers of small crafts, all of which together are the shore quarter, Maruvurppakkam.
silappathikaram:5:16-39.nuance: Line 21 (வளம்தலை மயங்கிய நனந்தலை மறுகும்) is word for word the closing line of the Pattinappaalai's list of goods pouring into Puhar (its line 193), so the epic's survey of the same city is built on the older poem's praise. The list names crafts and trades by the worker, not the guild or caste, and puts the bards (பெரும்பாண்) among the skilled trades.
silappathikaram:5:16-39.unit_note: Starts at line 16 (the weavers' item of lines 16-17) and ends at line 39, where மருவூர்ப் பாக்கமும் names and closes the whole first quarter; the core units broke at 32 and 47, inside the catalogue.

silappathikaram:5:40-58.reading: The second quarter, Pattinappakkam, is listed: the royal street and chariot street, the market square, the mansions of the great merchant families, the Brahmins' quarter, the farmers, the physicians and astrologers, the gem-setters and conch-cutters, the bards, heralds and panegyrists, the time-keepers, actors, courtesans and dancing women, flower-sellers and maids, drummers and players, jesters, and the horsemen, elephant-drivers, charioteers and fierce warriors camped round the palace.
silappathikaram:5:40-58.nuance: The inner town is ordered around the king: it opens on the royal and chariot streets and closes with the soldiers who ring the palace (இருந்துபுறம் சுற்றிய), with the courtesans (காவல் கணிகையர்) placed among the king's own servants, the world Madhavi belongs to.
silappathikaram:5:40-58.unit_note: Starts at line 40, the first item after மருவூர்ப் பாக்கமும் (line 39), and ends at line 58 (பட்டினப் பாக்கமும்), which names and closes the second quarter; the core units broke at 47 and 62.

silappathikaram:5:59-75.reading: Between the two quarters, like the no-man's-land between two kings' battle lines, lies the day market in a grove of close-set trees loud with buyers and sellers; there, when the month of Chittirai brings the full moon of Chitra, the women of the old warrior houses heap rice, cakes, flowers and incense on the altar of the guardian spirit that Indra sent to remove the king's trouble, dance possessed, and bless the king that hunger, disease and enmity may leave his land and plenty and abundance flow.
silappathikaram:5:59-75.nuance: The festival begins not with Indra but with the spirit he sent (தேவர் கோமான் ஏவலின் போந்த காவல் பூதம்), and with women who speak as possessed (வலவையின் உரைக்கும்): the blessing for the whole land is uttered in trance. The comparison of the market to the ground between two armies makes peace look like a truce.
silappathikaram:5:59-75.event: At the Chitra full moon the women of the warrior houses make offerings at the guardian spirit's altar, dance possessed and bless the king.
silappathikaram:5:59-75.unit_note: Starts at line 59, where the market between the two quarters is introduced (இருபெரு வேந்தர் முனையிடம் போல), and ends at line 75, where the old women's blessing closes (ஓதையின் பெயர); the core units broke at 62 and 80.

silappathikaram:5:76-88.reading: The fighting men of both quarters hurry first to the altar of the great sacrifice and, praying that the king's trouble be removed and that the offering be a bulwark of his strength, the slingers and spearmen who have won hard battles cut off their own dark heads with fierce reddened eyes, set them on the altar crying 'may the victorious king win', and with the thunder of the drum feed the spirit that eats life-offerings.
silappathikaram:5:76-88.nuance: The life-offering (உயிர்ப்பலி) here is the warriors' own heads offered for the king's victory; the narrator gives it no judgment, setting it among the festival's opening rites. The sense of 'cut off their heads' is taken from the head placed on the altar (கருந்தலை ... நற்பலி பீடிகை ... வைத்து); the verb itself is not stated.
silappathikaram:5:76-88.event: Warriors of both quarters offer their own heads at the altar for the king's victory.
silappathikaram:5:76-88.unit_note: Starts at line 76 with the warriors (மருவூர் மருங்கின் மறம்கொள் வீரரும்) and ends at line 88 (வான்பலி ஊட்டி), the end of their offering; the core units broke at 80 and 98.

silappathikaram:5:89-110.reading: The narrator recalls how Thirumavalavan, finding no match for his war-lust on earth, set out to the holy north with sword, umbrella and drum, asking that his arms find foes, and, stopped by the Himalaya, carved his tiger on its peak; on his way back the king of the Vajra land gave him a pavilion, the defeated king of Magadha a hall of debate, and the king of Avanti, gladly, an arched gate, gifts of gold and gems that no craftsman could make, made by Mayan, which now stand together in Puhar as a hall the great praise.
silappathikaram:5:89-110.nuance: The episode is told as the past (அந்நாள்), to explain monuments of the festival city; the king's name, திருமா வளவன், is the name of the Pattinappaalai's patron, and the Tamil supports no more than that shared name. The mountain halts him rather than any rival (பகைவிலக்கியது இப் பயம்கெழு மலை). Who received Mayan's help in lines 107-108 (அவர் தொல்லோர் உதவிக்கு) is not clear.
silappathikaram:5:89-110.event: Thirumavalavan goes north to the Himalaya, sets his tiger emblem there, and receives a pavilion, a debating hall and a gateway from three northern kings.
silappathikaram:5:89-110.unit_note: Starts at line 89 with Valavan's campaign (இருநில மருங்கின் பொருநரைப் பெறாஅ) and ends at line 110, where the three gifts are summed up as the hall the great praise (மண்டபம் அன்றியும்); the core units broke at 98 and 113.

silappathikaram:5:111-127.reading: Besides the hall, Puhar has the open court where traders' bundles marked with their names lie unguarded without lock or keeper, because any thief is made to carry his load on his head and whirl round; the court of the pool where the hunchbacked, dwarfs, dumb, deaf and lepers bathe, gain a flawless form and leave after circling it; and the court of the tall stone where those deceived and maddened, poisoned, snake-bitten or struck by demons come round, worship and are freed of their pain.
silappathikaram:5:111-127.nuance: The courts (மன்றம்) do the work of watchmen and physicians: theft is prevented by the place itself, and healing comes by circling and worship rather than by medicine. The city's safety is presented as a marvel, not as the king's police.
silappathikaram:5:111-127.unit_note: Starts at line 111 with the open court (வம்ப மாக்கள் தம்பெயர் பொறித்த) and ends at line 127 (நிழல்கால் நெடுங்கல் நின்ற மன்றமும்), closing the third court; the core units broke at 113 and 127.

silappathikaram:5:128-134.reading: At the crossroads of the spirit, a spirit roars across four kathams that hypocrites who hide behind penance, unchaste women who hide their wrong, ministers who betray, men who desire others' wives, false witnesses and backbiters will fall into the noose in its hand, and it beats and devours them.
silappathikaram:5:128-134.nuance: The spirit's list is a list of hidden wrongs: each kind of offender is one whose fault is concealed (மறைந்து ஒழுகும் twice), betrays a trust or speaks falsely behind others' backs, so the punishment exposes what ordinary justice cannot see.

claims.claim: hidden wrongdoers, the false ascetic, the unfaithful wife, the treacherous minister, the adulterer, the false witness and the backbiter, deserve to be seized and killed

silappathikaram:5:128-134.unit_note: Split the core unit 128-142 at line 134, where the crossroads of the spirit (பூத சதுக்கமும்) closes its item; the image court begins on line 135.

silappathikaram:5:135-140.reading: There is also the court of the image, where if the king's sceptre bends or a judge in the hall of justice bends the law-book and takes one side, the image weeps without a word; and in all five of these courts, praised by those who know the truth, rare offerings are made.
silappathikaram:5:135-140.nuance: The image weeps for two failures, not one: the king's bent sceptre and the judge who twists the treatise (உரைநூல் கோடி), so the court is a check on the king's justice and on his court's learning. It cannot speak or act (நாவொடு நவிலாது); it can only grieve.

claims.claim: when a king's sceptre bends or a judge leans to one side, the wrong is such that even a statue weeps

silappathikaram:5:135-140.unit_note: Split the core unit 128-142: starts at line 135 with the image court (அரைசுகோல் கோடினும்) and ends at line 140, where offerings in all five courts (ஐவகை மன்றத்தும் அரும்பலி உறீஇ) close the survey of the courts.

silappathikaram:5:141-156.reading: The festival drum is taken from the Vajra temple and set on the neck of an elephant, the start of the festival is proclaimed at the temple of the white elephant, the auspicious flag is raised to the sky at the temple of the wish-granting tree, and in every street the gates of the mansions are hung with pearl-mouthed arches, golden pots, lamps held by figures, banners, whisks and fragrant powder.
silappathikaram:5:141-156.event: The festival drum goes out on an elephant, the festival is proclaimed and its flag raised, and the streets are decorated.
silappathikaram:5:141-156.unit_note: Starts at line 141, the drum taken from the Vajra temple (வச்சிரக் கோட்டத்து மணம்கெழு முரசம்), and ends at line 156, where the street decoration closes (வீதியில் செறிந்துஆங்கு); the core units broke at 142 and 158.

silappathikaram:5:157-168.reading: The five great councils and the eight groups of attendants, princes, sons of merchants, horsemen, elephant-men and charioteers gather, wishing victory to the famed king, carry in golden pots the holy water of the Kaveri's great ford, and bathe the lord of the gods in it, to the wonder of earth and sky.
silappathikaram:5:157-168.nuance: Line 164 (ஆயிரத்து ஓர்எட்டு அரசுதலைக் கொண்ட) is unclear: it may describe the ford where a thousand and eight kings bathed, or the pots or kings who bear the water; the reading here leaves it open. The festival's central rite, the bathing of Indra, is performed by the king's councils on the king's behalf.
silappathikaram:5:157-168.event: The king's councils and attendants bathe Indra's image in Kaveri water carried in golden pots.
silappathikaram:5:157-168.unit_note: Starts at line 157 with the councils (ஐம்பெருங் குழுவும்) and ends at line 168 (விண்ணவர் தலைவனை விழுநீர் ஆட்டி), the bathing of Indra; the core units broke at 158 and 173.

silappathikaram:5:169-186.reading: In the temples of the Unborn One, of six-faced Murugan, of the white-bodied elder brother, of the dark tall god and of the king of the white umbrella, on one side Vedic fire rites follow the ancient way; on another the many classes of gods each have their festival; on another the monasteries of the virtuous and the alms-halls give charity as the wise prescribe; on another kings who would not join the Chola are freed from their fetters; and on another musicians, lute-players and bards make music.
silappathikaram:5:169-186.nuance: The repeated ஒருபால் ('on one side') sets Vedic sacrifice, the gods' festivals, the charity of the அறவோர் பள்ளி and the release of captive kings side by side without ranking them; the release of the fettered kings is called grace (அருள்). The temple of the 'king of the white umbrella' may be Indra's or a royal shrine; the Tamil does not say.
silappathikaram:5:169-186.event: Rites of every kind go on at once in Puhar's temples, and captive kings are released.
silappathikaram:5:169-186.unit_note: Starts at line 169 with the temples (பிறவா யாக்கைப் பெரியோன் கோயிலும்) and ends at line 186, the last ஒருபால் clause; line 187 begins the sentence of the festival streets that leads to Kovalan, so it goes with the next unit. The core units broke at 173 and 187.

silappathikaram:5:187-207.reading: In the festive streets where the drums never sleep, the southern breeze wanders with the bees and the young spring like Kovalan, who roams with Madhavi, garlanded in jasmine and lily, a woman never parted from her lover to become the talk of the town, delighting in love, bathing in groves, entering new flower gardens, with bards and town gallants; and the onlookers begin to wonder whether the moon itself, carrying a dark cloud and painting two dark carp with a kumizh flower between them, has come down to wander here for fear of the serpent in the sky.
silappathikaram:5:187-207.nuance: Kovalan enters the chapter only inside a simile, as the measure of the spring wind's wandering (திரிதரு மரபின் கோவலன் போல), and Madhavi is praised as one who has never been parted from her beloved (காதல் கொழுநனைப் பிரிந்துஅலர் எய்தா), the word கொழுநன், a husband, given to the man who is Kannaki's. The question at lines 204-207 opens a run of wonderings closed by என at line 223; who wonders is not named, and whether the face like the moon is Madhavi's or any festival beauty's is not fixed.
silappathikaram:5:187-207.event: Kovalan roams the festival streets and gardens with Madhavi.
silappathikaram:5:187-207.unit_note: Starts at line 187 (முழவுக்கண் துயிலாது முடுக்கரும் வீதியும்), which with line 188 sets the scene for Kovalan's wandering, and ends at line 207, the first question closed by உண்டுகொல்; the core unit began at 188.

silappathikaram:5:208-217.reading: The wondering goes on: does the heavenly creeper that Kama grew, nourished on the moon's nectar, come here too, and, as if Lakshmi had entered the city to show the king its wealth, does a false lotus wander here with ilavam, mullai, kuvalai and kumizh blooming on it, seeking a partner in its painted disguise?
silappathikaram:5:208-217.nuance: Each question turns a woman's face into a thing out of place: a creeper from heaven, a lotus walking the streets, its flowers being lips, teeth, eyes and nose. The 'disguise' (உள்வரி கோலம்) suggests the festival's masked or costumed women; the speakers are still the unnamed onlookers.

silappathikaram:5:218-234.reading: Or, they ask, has Death, which drinks many lives, afraid that the king's sceptre will forbid its work, changed its manly form but not its deadly task, and come wandering as a woman with a modest look, a smiling face and a voice like the lute; and against those it meets, Kama's great bodiless army fights, painting their bodies with love's lines, while the wives of Arundhati-like chastity, living with husbands who came home with guests, tremble helpless, wondering whether the earth holds any cure if the red-cornered glance of their eyes does not end with the guest.
silappathikaram:5:218-234.nuance: The conceit makes the king's just rule the reason women are deadly: under the Chola's sceptre Death cannot kill openly, so it kills as a woman. The last lines (227-234) are hard: whose eye wounds whom, and whether the wives fear their husbands' new loves or suffer their own longing, is not clear from the Tamil.

claims.claim: under a king whose sceptre is just, Death cannot do its work openly

silappathikaram:5:218-234.unit_note: Split the core unit 218-240 at line 234, which ends the wondering and the wives' fear with the festival's midday (நல்வினை நடுநாள்); the omen of the two women's eyes begins on line 235.

silappathikaram:5:235-240.reading: Like a red lily whose heart is so full of pollen that it trembles and spills its honey, Kannaki's dark eyes and Madhavi's red eyes, hiding what filled them within, shed tears, and throbbed, in that order, the left and the right, on the day of the festival of the king of the gods.
silappathikaram:5:235-240.nuance: The eyes throb 'in the order counted' (எண்ணுமுறை), so the left goes with Kannaki, named first, and the right with Madhavi; read as omens for women, the wife's is the good sign of a husband's return and the courtesan's the bad sign of parting. The chapter's festival thus closes on the two women together, each weeping, at the moment of their fortunes' turn.
silappathikaram:5:235-240.event: On the festival day Kannaki's left eye and Madhavi's right eye throb and both weep.
silappathikaram:5:235-240.unit_note: Split the core unit 218-240: starts at line 235, a new sentence with its own simile (உள்அகம் நறுந்தாது), and ends at line 240, the chapter's close.

links.note: The epic's line 21, வளம்தலை மயங்கிய நனந்தலை மறுகும், is the Pattinappaalai's line 193 on the same city's streets of mingled wealth.
links.teaches: Pattinappaalai uses the line to close a map of goods arriving from every mountain and sea, while the epic attaches it to a census of Puhar's own craftsmen and traders, so the borrowed praise moves from what flows into the port to who works in it.

gains.a: its catalogue is anchored in an older poem's praise of the same streets, which tells the reader this is the canonical Puhar
gains.b: the older line gains a list of the people behind the wealth, whom its own poem leaves out

links.note: Pattinappaalai's Thirumavalavan makes the northerners wilt among many regional conquests; the epic's Thirumavalavan marches to the Himalaya and brings back gifts from three named northern kings.
links.teaches: Read together, the two show a Sangam king's memory being enlarged: one line of the older poem about the north becomes a whole campaign whose trophies are buildings in Puhar, so the epic makes the conquest serve its picture of the city.

gains.a: the epic's past king gains a Sangam record under the same name, showing the episode draws on remembered praise
gains.b: the poem's brief line on the northerners gains a later tradition that turned it into a Himalayan expedition

links.note: Purananuru 66 praises Karikal Valavan's victory at Venni but says the defeated king who fasted to death for shame at his back wound is better than he; the epic's Valavan is checked by no rival, only by the Himalaya.
links.teaches: The Purananuru sets a moral limit on the victor through the vanquished man's honour, while the epic removes every human limit and lets only a mountain halt him, so the later memory of the Chola has lost the Sangam poet's check on royal glory.

gains.a: the epic's war-lust with no rival left gains a contrast that shows what its praise omits
gains.b: the poem's lesson that the defeated may be the better man gains a later portrait in which no such man remains

links.note: The blessing பசியும் பிணியும் பகையும் நீங்கி வசியும் வளனும் சுரக்க is uttered in both: here by possessed old women at the spirit's altar, in Manimekalai by the royal drummer announcing the festival.
links.teaches: The same two lines pass from the trance speech of warrior women at a spirit's altar to the official proclamation of the king's crier, showing the sequel turning a possessed blessing into the festival's civic formula.

links.note: Manimekalai's councils warn that if the festival is forgotten, the spirit that relieved the king and the spirit that beats and eats wrongdoers bound in its noose will not stay.
links.teaches: The Silappathikaram presents the crossroads spirit as a standing marvel of Puhar, while the Manimekalai makes its presence depend on keeping Indra's festival, so the city's moral guard becomes something that can be lost by neglect.

links.note: The spirit's first victims are those who hide behind penance (தவம்மறைந்து ஒழுகும்); Kural 274 likens hiding in penance to a hunter hiding in a bush to snare birds.
links.teaches: The Kural shows why the false ascetic's concealment is dangerous, that it lets him prey on others, but names no penalty; the epic imagines a city where the concealment is publicly broken and punished with death, setting a sanction beside the couplet's diagnosis.

gains.a: the spirit's list gains the couplet's reason why the hidden ascetic is the worst of wrongdoers
gains.b: the couplet gains a civic answer to the hidden hunter, a power that sees through the bush

links.note: Puhar has an image that weeps when the sceptre bends; in Madurai the Pandya's sceptre bends and he himself declares 'I am the thief' and dies.
links.teaches: Puhar's check on a bent sceptre is an image that can only weep, while Madurai has no such image and the king must find and judge his own fault at the cost of his life, so the epic moves from a ritual sign of injustice to its full price.

links.note: Kural 559: if the king bends justice the sky bends and withholds rain; the epic's image weeps when either the king's sceptre or the judge's reading bends.
links.teaches: Both make a mute power answer a bent justice, but the Kural's answer punishes the whole land through the rain while the epic's image only grieves, and the epic adds a second culprit, the judge who twists the law-book, which the couplet does not consider.

gains.a: the weeping image gains the Kural's claim that a bent sceptre has consequences beyond the court
gains.b: the couplet gains the point that justice can be bent by the king's judges as well as by the king

links.note: Kural 1083's lover learns that Death has a woman's form; the epic says Death took a woman's form because the king's just sceptre forbade its killing.
links.teaches: The Kural's conceit of the deadly beauty is a lover's discovery, while the epic gives it a political cause, the sceptre that holds Death in check, so a love-figure is turned into praise of the king.

gains.a: the epic's wonder gains the Kural's established conceit of Death in a woman's grace
gains.b: the couplet's figure gains a reason inside a just kingdom, why Death must disguise itself

links.note: Kannaki's left eye throbs at the festival; in Kaathai 9 a servant announces that Kovalan has come home.
links.teaches: The good omen is fulfilled in Kovalan's return, but the return leads at once to the journey to Madurai, so the sign of reunion is also the first step toward his death.

links.note: Madhavi's right eye throbs at the festival; at the end of the Kaanal Vari Kovalan, his former deeds come to fruit, lets go of her and leaves.
links.teaches: The bad omen given to Madhavi on Indra's festival is fulfilled at the seashore at the festival's end, where the story names former deeds as the cause, so the omen and the karma explanation frame the same parting from two sides.

new_concepts.gloss: the festival; a public feast of a god or a town

Line 164 (ஆயிரத்து ஓர்எட்டு அரசுதலைக் கொண்ட) is obscure as it stands: it is unclear whether the thousand and eight are kings, pots or fords.
Lines 227-234: the construction of the chaste wives' fear is hard to parse and may be corrupt or elliptical.
